definition.text: The pelagic zone is the water column of the open ocean, away from the shore and the seabed.

facts.text: Down the water column pressure rises, temperature and light fall, and salinity, oxygen and nutrients change.
The pelagic ecosystem is based on phytoplankton, which need sunlight and so live in the upper sunlit layer.
Biodiversity drops sharply below the sunlit layer as oxygen, food and light dwindle and pressure and cold increase.
Pelagic fish are often migratory forage fish such as herring and anchovies, plus the larger predators such as tuna and sharks that follow them.
About 80% of ocean carbon fixation happens in the open ocean, which covers more than 90% of the ocean area.

definition.text: The open ocean is divided by depth into five layers: epipelagic, mesopelagic, bathypelagic, abyssopelagic and hadopelagic.

facts.text: The sunlit epipelagic zone is the only layer with enough light for photosynthesis; nearly all ocean primary production and about 90% of marine life is there.
The twilight mesopelagic zone gets only trace sunlight, and many of its animals use bioluminescence or rise to the surface at night to feed.
In the pitch-black bathypelagic zone most animals live on 'marine snow', detritus falling from above.
The hadal zone, below 6,000 m in trenches, reaches 10,935 m at Challenger Deep, with pressures of 1,100 atm.

definition.text: In the ocean the biomass pyramid is inverted at its base: consumers such as copepods, krill and forage fish outweigh the primary producers.

facts.text: Ocean producers are tiny, fast-reproducing phytoplankton, so a small mass yields high production, while land producers like mature forests need far more mass for the same output.
As a result zooplankton make up most marine animal biomass and link phytoplankton to the rest of the food web.

definition.text: River ecosystems are flowing waters that drain the landscape, with their living organisms and the physical and chemical conditions they interact with.

facts.text: They form networks in which small headwater streams feed mid-size streams and then large rivers.
One-way water flow is the key factor shaping river ecology; fast, turbulent water holds more oxygen and supports more biodiversity than slow pools.
Large rivers have more species than small streams, linked to their greater area, volume and habitat variety.
Pollution, from fertiliser and sewage to plastics, drugs, road salt and heat, can cut ecosystem functioning, services, biodiversity and human health.
Dams change flow, temperature and sediment, fragment rivers and block migrating fish.

title: River continuum concept

definition.text: The river continuum concept is a framework describing how temperate river ecosystems change in function from small headwaters to large rivers.

facts.text: It uses stream order to measure position along the gradient from small stream to large river.
Small shaded headwaters depend on leaf litter from land, mid-sized rivers get enough light for algae, and large rivers rely again mainly on outside inputs.
Animal communities track the energy supply: shredders thrive in small streams and grazers at mid-order sites.
Critics argue it rests on small temperate streams and cannot explain systems that switch between flowing and still states, which the flood pulse concept covers.

contested_note: Junk et al. argue the concept was built on small temperate streams and has been wrongly applied to all river systems.
